newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Gulf Arabs to wait and see on Iran's Khatami.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs to wait and see on Iran's Khatami.

text.p: Gulf Arab states are mostly glad that Iran elected a moderate to the presidency but regional hardliners fear he might not bring about much change in Tehran's policy, Gulf and Western official sources said.
"Our problem with Iran is trust," said a Gulf source on Tuesday. "Do not expect a rush towards Khatami. I think most Gulf states will adopt a wait-and-see policy."
Gulf Arab states have followed diplomatic protocol and sent Khatami congratulatory cables on his victory.

But in Gulf Arab power broker Saudi Arabia and elsewhere in the region, some argue that outgoing President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani was first hailed as a pragmatist but that after two terms, ties are still marred by suspicions and that he failed to contain what they see as extremists.
"There are some who feel there no moderates in Iran...They might be moderate compared to the alternative," one source said.
A senior Western political adviser who toured the region said: "Saudi believes Iran was somehow involved in the Khobar bombing" which killed 19 U.S. airmen in the kingdom last year.
"Proof of Iran's involvement in terrorism is plenty but how high up was the state involved in Khobar, if at all, is a matter yet to be seen," he added.

Iran often denies support for terrorism or a role in the Khobar attack. Riyadh has not accused Tehran or any party of the bombing although there have been Western media reports, seen by some sources as official leaks, hinting at Iran's involvement.

"They are happy that Khatami won and are also glad that Rafsanjani will continue to play a significant role in the future," a Gulf source said of Riyadh's moderate camp which sources link to Crown Prince Abdullah.
He was referring to recent "assurances" by Iran that Rafsanjani would play an official and key role, including in foreign policy, after stepping down as president.

But the other camp, mainly linked to King Fahd's full brothers who hold key posts, is pursuing several leads in the Khobar investigation which apparently point towards Iran's possible involvement, Arab and Western sources said.
Before the election non-Arab Iran used its hosting next December of an Islamic summit to tour several Arab states to present invitations and try to ease some of the tension.

Although the initiative was seen by some as a good first step towards confidence building, Egypt showed Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati documents which it said proved Tehran's role in political violence.

Velayati's meeting with King Fahd was cold compared to talks with the crown prince while the United Arab Emirates received him with a cold shoulder, said diplomats, adding that Abu Dhabi was expected to issue a response to remarks by Rafsanjani and Khatami in a war of words over disputed Gulf islands.
